# Lomasakassapajātaka (Ja 433)

**ID:** Ja 433  
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Lomasakassapajātaka  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul8.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul8.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Lomasakassapajātaka* (Ja 433) is a Jātaka narrative set at Jetavana, where the Buddha delivers the discourse concerning a discontented or worldly-minded monk (*ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu*), warning that defilements can debase even beings of supreme purity [Fausböll 1883]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta renounced the world to lead an austere ascetic life in the Himalayas; known as Lomasakassapa ("Hairy Kassapa"), his rigorous austerities threatened the position of the god Sakka [Cowell 1897]. To break the hermit's virtue, Sakka appeared to the king of Benares, promising him universal sovereignty free from aging and death if he brought Lomasakassapa to perform an animal sacrifice, encapsulated by the opening verse *Assa Inda-samo rājā* ("A king like Indra thou shalt be") [Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897]. In the conclusion (*samodhāna*), the royal minister Sayha is identified with Sāriputta and the ascetic Lomasakassapa with the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1883].

This episode—in which the Bodhisatta is induced to prepare a massive animal sacrifice after becoming infatuated with the king's daughter Candavatī—is famously discussed as a quandary in the *Milindapañha* (Mil 5.5.5, *Buddhaaviheṭhakapañha*), which explains that the Bodhisatta acted while beside himself with passion rather than with lucid, malicious intent [Endo 1997; Dalton 2011]. Within the Pali commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), the text is frequently cited alongside stories such as the *Haritajātaka* and *Mudulakkhaṇajātaka* as a cautionary exemplar of ascetics forfeiting their meditative attainments (*jhāna*) through heedlessness and lust [Fausböll 1883; Fausböll 1891].

- Passage-level parallels: Ja 310 Seyyajātaka; Ja 309 Chavakajātaka; Bu-Vb Sk69 Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Sekhiya 69; Ja 287 Lābhagarahajātaka
- Mentioned in: Mil 5.5.5 Buddhaaviheṭhakapañha

**Sources**

- [Fausböll 1891] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka together with its Commentary, Vol. 5 (1891) — Provided commentary citations grouping Lomasakassapa with other stories of falling from jhāna.
- [Cowell 1897] E. B. Cowell (ed.), The Jātaka or Stories of the Buddha's Former Births, Vol. 3 (1897) — Provided English narrative details concerning Sakka, the animal sacrifice, and verse reuse in Ja 310.
